newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Unemployment still clouds French economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Unemployment still clouds French economy.

text.p: France's economy expanded by 1.5 percent in 1996, more than previously forecast, according to data published on Tuesday which also underpinned the view that there should be a gradual pick-up this year.

While the centre-right government will welcome the news a month from a parliamentary election, it faces further figures on Wednesday expected to show the unemployment rate stuck stubbornly at a record 12.8 percent.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Tuesday predicted growth should create between 120,000 and 140,000 jobs this year and the unemployment trend should soon go into reverse. But he conceded this would not happen in coming months.

"I know that for a few more months there will still be a considerable number of people entering the labour market for the first time. We know that in the coming months there will not be a downward turn in unemployment," Arthuis said in a debate with Socialist former finance minister Michel Sapin.
"But we are in a turnaround phase, we're on the eve of job creation which is estimated at 250,000 for 1998," he said on LCI television.

The national statistics institute, INSEE, said on Tuesday it had revised upwards its initial estimates of 1.3 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996. It also announced that consumer spending had come in flat in March.

Economists said the revision of last year's economic growth figures was largely technical but the other data comforted their view of healthier consumer spending over the first quarter of this year and, in turn, their view that the overall economy should pick up gradually later this year.
INSEE said France's public deficit for 1996 came in at 4.2 percent of GDP, slightly above a government forecast of 4.1 percent.

Economists said there appeared to be discrepancies in the INSEE figures but a senior finance ministry official said the public deficit was still 4.2 percent, or 380 billion francs ($65.2 billion), when calculated in line with the Maastricht treaty on European monetary union.

The government has vowed to cut the public deficit to three percent of GDP in 1997, the target limit set under the Maastricht treaty to qualify for the launch of a single euro currency, planned for January 1, 1999.
Economic indicators since the start of this year have been mixed but economists believe an upturn is on the way and this was reinforced by Tuesday's consumer spending data.

"The consumer spending data is more interesting, it's as expected, that represents a rise of three percent on an annual basis in the first quarter," said David Naude, Paris economist for U.S. investment bank JP Morgan.
"We're saying there will be a recovery but it will be slow. The underlying trend is improvement but a slow one, especially in the first half," he said.
The government is forecasting minimum economic growth of 2.3 percent this year and 2.8 percent in 1998.

The blackspot remains unemployment, with most recent data showing nearly 3.1 million jobless at the end of February -- one in three of them out of work for more than a year and one in five of them under 25 years old.

Former finance minister Sapin reiterated a Socialist programme of creating 700,000 jobs with government backing, half of them in the public sector. He also said the policy of the opposition Socialist party was to boost consumer spending and that this was more important than the gradual income tax cuts started by the centre-right government in its 1996 budget.

INSEE's revised growth data for 1996 showed a 1.6 percent rise in consumer spending over the previous year but showed that business investment, seen as a key point of weakness in the economy, fell by 0.5 percent and actually dragged GDP down.
